messages.subject: compare.evol.rates significance method
parts:
Hi, I´m using the function compare.evol.rates to test if there are significant differences in rates between two groups (geometric morphometric data). The thing is I´m not sure which method for assessing significance should I use. When I used "simulation" my results where not significant (p>0.05), but when i try the "permutation" method i got significant differences (p<0.05).

Thanks in advance

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Re: compare.evol.rates significance method
parts:
Juan,

 

That is certainly not a huge number of species for such a comparison. The algebra will ‘work’, but I’d be very cautious with my interpretation, regardless of the method used to assess significance.

 

I suspect that you have many more variables than sample size (N = 8); meaning that your data do not occupy or ‘fill up’ the morphospace very well. Thus, spurious statistical results are likely. This may be one reason why results differ under simulation versus permutation. For the latter, it uses the same 8 shapes re-assigned to different branches of the tree for testing significance. Whereas for the former, the method simulates data under Brownian motion, and across many runs it may investigate more components of morphospace than your original 8 specimens; thereby leading to a result that states the groups are not overly different as compared to a random selection of phenotypes in morphospace.  When interpreting such patterns I tend to be more conservative, and state up-front the caveats of my dataset (in this case, a small number of specimens relative to variables).

 

Of course, something we always advocate is an investigation of the effect size of any statistical test: not just reliance on p-values. If the effect size is quite large, then this provides important information for interpreting the patterns biologically. Mike and I have discussed this at length in this forum in previous posts: whether it be for interpreting linear model effects, modularity / integration signal, or results from phylogenetic comparative methods. I recommend that here also.

 

Good luck!

Dean
